content.thinking:
I'm picturing a koala sized around 0.7 meters sitting height, gripping a eucalyptus branch mounted on a freestanding base so it can stand on the floor—like a Y-shaped fork of branch where the koala nestles into the crook.

Working out the pose and structure: a vertical trunk rising from a stump base, with an angled side branch, and the koala perched at the fork with its arms wrapped around the wood in the classic clinging posture. I'm weighing whether the koala should face forward with limbs gripping a trunk piece directly in front of it versus clinging from the side, trying to land on something stable and visually readable from the front.

I'll settle on the classic pose: the koala straddles a branch extending forward from the trunk along Z at height y=0.40, legs hanging on either side, with arms wrapped around the trunk itself rather than a separate handhold branch — simpler and more recognizable.

I'll grow a second branch from the trunk near the top, curving forward and down into an arc so the koala's hands can wrap around it at chest height, with leaves at the tip.

I'm reconsidering the branch orientation so the koala can hug it naturally, running it forward along Z from the trunk so both arms wrap around it with hands meeting underneath, rather than a T-shaped junction which wouldn't look like real eucalyptus branches.

Facing the koala directly toward the trunk also fails since the front-view camera would see the trunk blocking the koala's body and face. A better setup might have the koala sitting in a fork of the tree, facing forward, with arms gripping a lower branch at belly height instead.

Actually, a Y-fork feels more natural: the trunk splits near the top into two limbs diverging outward, and the koala sits nestled in the crotch of the fork with each arm wrapped around one of the branching limbs, its body framed between them.

Still working out limb positions...

Checking the gap at the inner surface confirms it's good. For arms, I'm positioning the shoulder and hand so fingers wrap around the limb like digit capsules, and for legs I'm placing the hips near the seat/crotch area to keep proportions consistent.

I need to pull the trunk back a bit so the koala's body doesn't intersect it — moving the trunk base further in z so the crotch sits clear, then positioning the pelvis and chest capsules so there's a slight, acceptable overlap with the trunk at the back.

For the legs, I'm working out how a sitting koala's knees bend forward and where the feet should grip the limb below — testing a few placements near the hip and settling on feet gripping the branch around y=0.50, x≈±0.19, since dangling straight down looked anatomically off.

I'm overthinking the geometry here, so let me switch to a more empirical approach: sketch an IK limb with bends, preview it, then adjust. I'll try having the legs hang forward in a sitting pose, with feet gripping a short branch stub, and work out approximate hip, knee, and ankle coordinates for each leg.

I'm checking that these leg lengths are reasonable — short thighs and shins make sense since koala hind legs are compact — and now I'm tracing where the fork limb actually bends relative to the trunk to make sure the foot placement lines up.

I'm continuing to plot the limb path so it curves forward and outward at a low angle before tipping down to the foot, with the koala's grip landing around the right z-depth. Then I think about where the koala's seat rests in the crotch of the fork and how the trunk base meets the plinth disc.

Realizing the whole sculpture is too squat, I decide to raise everything by shifting the fork, seat, and head heights upward, bringing the branch stand to roughly 1.6m and the koala itself to around 0.7m sitting. For scale, I settle on the koala's head being about 0.16m wide with chunky, oversized round ears and nose typical of pixel art, and work out a texel size that gives a reasonable pixel resolution for a figure this size.

For the plinth, I plan an octagonal log-slice base with bark texture, roots, grass tufts, fallen eucalyptus leaves, and a gum nut cluster on a soil-and-grass top. I'll lean on cellPaint textures for the fur gradient and bark rather than flat color counts, keeping things within a reasonable color budget.

Now I'm laying out the joint skeleton starting from a pelvis root, through a spine chain, neck, head, jaw, ear hinges, and arm chains down to shoulder, elbow, wrist, and finger digits.

For the head, I'm thinking round fluffy ears, a big oval nose, and using low-segment spheres with cellPaint shading to keep that blocky, stair-stepped pixel look rather than smooth geometry.

Eyes get small pixelated boxes with black fill and a tiny white glint, nose is a rounded black box with highlight texels, and ears are built from stepped circle extrudes—grey outer fur with a fluffy white inner layer.

Fur card tufts line the ear rims and chest for texture, using a dithered grayscale paint ramp with vertical fur streaks and randomized light/dark specks for strand variation. I'm mapping lighter patches for chest, belly, and ears, darker tones for arms, and a pale spotted pattern on the rump based on position rules.

Now I'm adding eucalyptus leaf cards hanging in clusters at branch tips, long slender blue-green pixel-textured leaves, alongside smooth gum bark painted with mottled tan/grey/pink/olive streaks and peeling bark ribbon strips along the branch tubes.

For the base, I'm planning a cylindrical plinth with normal-based cellPaint, topped with a soil mound, grass tuft cards, scattered leaf cards lying flat, small sphere gumnuts, pebbles, and maybe a bark curl — keeping decorations thematically tied to eucalyptus and koala habitat while skipping any text/signage since pixel text would be awkward to render.

Now I'm working out koala anatomy: chunky capsule-shaped digits with pale claw spikes, five fingers per forepaw mimicking the real opposable-thumb grouping, and hind feet with fused toes and claws. I'm also setting the posture with a slight backward lean against the trunk and a forward head tilt, working out the coordinates for the head position relative to the trunk fork.

Still writing trunk and limb coordinates...

Now I'm adding a third thin trunk branch going left at the back for extra leaf mass, then moving to the koala itself: setting the pelvis position, defining the body as a sweeping capsule spine from pelvis through mid to chest with tapering radii to get that chubby koala build, and figuring out limb placement relative to the body's width.

Widening the fork limbs slightly so the arms can wrap properly, then calculating overall koala height from butt to head top—around 0.72, a bit large but reasonable for a sitting adult koala. Now I'm positioning the head on the neck, sizing it with width, height, and depth proportions plus a snout, and nudging the dimensions up a bit since the chibi style calls for an oversized head.

Now I'm placing the facial features: a chunky rounded-rectangle nose at the front, disk-shaped ears tilted outward with white inner detail, and small eyes positioned symmetrically. I'm also setting up the shoulders and arm limbs, defining hand positions and limb lengths with a bend hint so the elbows angle outward and down.

Working out finger geometry wrapping around the limb, with digit chains curving from the palm around the outer side of the limb.

Still working out hand geometry...

Checking the shoulder-to-hand distance, the arm segments are too long for the reach, forcing an awkward elbow bend outward. I should spread the limbs further apart instead—widening the hand position and shoulder placement so the koala's grasping pose looks more natural rather than tightly folded.

Checking whether the arm placement clips into the ear or cheek region, and nudging head depth slightly forward of the arms to avoid visible overlap. Settling on the upper limb path starting near the shoulder point.

Mapping out the arm's path from shoulder through elbow to hand, leaning outward then curving back near the top, plus roughly positioning the hip, knee, and foot for the leg.

I'm working through the foot wrap and ankle fold against the limb, letting the IK solver handle the knee bend with a forward-out-up hint. Then I'm checking whether the pelvis position would overlap with the trunk geometry and adjusting its z-depth to avoid penetration.

Shifting the whole koala forward slightly so the pelvis clears the trunk face, and aligning hand positions with the limb z-coordinates. I'm adding a small pale rump bump for the tail stub and starting to plan the fur color palette, moving from dark charcoal tones through mid-greys to pale highlights.

Now I'm settling on a cooler grey-brown fur ramp instead of pinkish tones, with black nose and highlight, cream and pink ear interiors, dark eyes, and pale claws. I'm also sketching the bark palette with warm creams and olive greys plus rust-orange peeling patches, and starting on leaf greens.

For the plinth, I'm planning a stepped lathe shape with eight segments to get a pixel-stair effect, painted with wood rings and soil strata on the sides and grass/moss/dirt on top, sitting at a small base radius. For the eucalyptus foliage, I'm thinking of using small pixel-art leaf textures on hanging cards clustered at twig tips, with hundreds of leaves kept cheap, plus a branch stand to support it all.

For fur, I'm planning scattered pixel tuft cards in grey and cream tones for the chest, cheeks, and ear rims, spaced with minimum distance constraints for natural coverage. For the head, I'm sculpting a scaled sphere with cell-paint shading to lighten the muzzle area and add realistic face tone variation around the nose and mouth.

Now I'm thinking through the body shape using a swept spine chain with elliptical cross-sections, painting a cream belly patch versus a darker back, with shading based on surface normals plus noise streaks to get that hand-painted pixel-art banding look. I'm laying out the spine joints from pelvis through chest as a Catmull-Rom path.

Still defining skeleton structure...

Counting joint totals across digits and legs, I land around 90 joints total, well under the 160 cap. For the digits I'm planning thin sweeps with small claw spikes at the tips, and dark charcoal naked-skin paws at the wrist like real koala pads, with fur layered on top. I still need to work out the head's skin sphere and double-check chain orientations visually once previewed.

Now I'm shaping the head itself as a slightly flattened skull sphere, adding fluffy white cheek puffs on the sides, and a lighter muzzle sphere for the short broad koala snout. I'm placing a prominent black box-shaped nose at the front-top of the muzzle, positioning the small close-set eyes just above and to either side of it, adding a tiny mouth line beneath, and building a separate lower jaw piece as a flattened sphere hinged at a jaw joint under the muzzle.

I'm figuring out the best way to orient and texture the nose -- deciding between a plain colored box versus adding a decal plane for highlights, since a textured box geometry would just repeat the same image on every face rather than giving a clean front-facing nose look.

Designing nose texture with nostril slits, and planning eyes as tiny black boxes with a single white glint pixel, nestled into the head sphere so they don't float or clip through the curved surface.

For the ear tufts, I'm working out stepped circular outlines by computing row spans across cells so the extruded shape approximates a circle of the right radius, ready to turn into actual geometry code.

Still defining ear geometry...

I need earL/earR joints parented to head with hinge roles, and must explicitly set bone references on the ring cards and branch sweeps since the literal geometry won't auto-bind to the nearest joint correctly otherwise. For bark coloring, I'm using noise sampled from position and normal to create vertical streak patterns.

For peeling bark patches, I'm thresholding a second noise channel to swap in rust, orange, and olive tones, plus adding dark speckles and scribble-like marks to mimic knots and scarring on eucalyptus-style bark.

I'm estimating the texture atlas budget — figuring out texel density needed across the total painted surface area to keep cells sharp without wasting resolution, and it looks like roughly 15 flat colors and a 1024 sheet should comfortably cover branches and bark detail.

For finer features like a koala's face, I'm deciding on varying cell sizes per body part rather than one uniform texel size — something like 0.016 for the body, 0.008 for facial detail, and 0.02 for trunk and leaf cards, so small areas get crisper resolution without blowing up the whole atlas.

Now I'm setting up the actual code: importing the builder, frame, math, and path utilities along with the pixel-paint kit helpers, then thinking through palette normalization — possibly snapping colors to a fixed number of levels for retro coherence.

Writing fur shader function...

Now I'm designing a reusable fur-paint function that different body parts (body, head, arms, legs) can share, each supplying their own bias. I'm sketching the body's sweep path as a set of center points with varying ellipse radii to shape the koala's belly bulge and pelvis width.

I'm realizing the bottom cap of the body would sink too low, ending up floating in front of the trunk fork rather than resting between the limbs, so I need to adjust where the sweep starts or shift the body up to align properly with the leg attachment points.

Checking the head placement above the chest, I get a total koala height from feet to head-top of about 0.82, which feels a bit tall for a sitting pose closer to 0.7 — I'm considering scaling things down slightly to keep the chibi proportions chunky but compact.

Now I'm working out joint positions for the limbs: shoulders, elbows, and feet along the arm path, then the hip and leg geometry. Checking the hip-to-ankle distance, I find it's only about 0.07 units, which is far too short for the thigh and shin segment lengths I planned (0.16 and 0.14), meaning the legs would end up way too folded and need adjusting.

Checking the leg fold geometry against real koala sitting posture—knees should jut forward and up, so I'm shifting the knee joint to about (s*0.2, 0.62, 0.15), keeping thigh length near .19 from hip and verifying the shin segment reaches the ankle target.

Still shaping limb curve...

Now I'm sketching the overall scene scale, about 1.75m tall including foliage, and planning secondary twigs branching off the main limbs at various points with their own tapering radii and leaf placements.

I'm figuring out leaf placement along those twigs — curved, sickle-shaped eucalyptus leaves hanging downward as pixel-textured cards, aiming for roughly 300 total across the structure, plus gumnut clusters as small merged spheres with caps. I'm also adding detail to the trunk: a broken stub with peeling bark curls, a knot, moss at the base, and exposed roots before moving on to the plinth.

For the plinth I'm lathing a stepped cylindrical outline with wood-toned sides and a patchy grass-and-dirt top, scattered with pebbles, grass tufts, fallen leaf cards, and a small mushroom cluster for charm, plus a tilted plaque stone on the front carved with a pixel leaf emblem.

Now I'm sketching the leaf glyph for the plaque texture, drawing it with the stem anchored at the bottom row since the card hangs with its root edge attached there, making the tip point upward in the finished drawing.

Now I'm planning out the rest of the texture set: fur tufts with tapering triangular shapes in grey and cream variants, grass blade tufts, a fallen leaf variant reusing the leaf shape rotated flat, and a bark peel strip texture.

Then I'm working through the fur card placement logic—rings of cards for ears flowing outward, and scattered body fur cards with size, lean, and bend parameters controlling how fur flows down and back across the koala's form.

For texture, I realize I can tint fur cards using the local color paint at each root, letting a grey-ramp tuft texture multiply against fur color so highlights stay light and shadows go darker. Now I need to actually write the implementation, being careful with the typed builder API signatures for cards and textures.

Writing digit chain generator...

Adding claw spikes at digit tips, then building the arm chain with shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints as a tapered sweep. I'm setting paw skin to a dark color and handling side naming so left and right mirror correctly along the X axis.

Now I'm constructing the leg limb with hip, knee, and ankle joints, bending the inner knee joint and attaching five toes around the foot. I'm positioning the hip joint as a child of the pelvis spine joint, offset outward by side.

Then I set up the neck chain into a head joint and a separate jaw joint, both aiming forward, before placing head and jaw parts in local model space without extra rotation. I'm scaling a sphere for the head shape, stretching it wider than tall to get the right proportions.

Next I'm working out the muzzle as a smaller, lighter-colored sphere positioned on the front-lower face, then adding a box-shaped nose stacked on top of the muzzle front, calculating the exact z-depths so the nose sits flush with the muzzle's leading edge. For the eyes I'm solving for the correct surface z-position using the head sphere's implicit equation so the eye sockets sit naturally on the curved head surface rather than floating or sinking in.

Setting up ear joint hinges and a helper function to compute normal/tangent directions for extruding the ear outline along the correct axis.

With the inner radius set, I'm giving it a cream color dithered pink toward the center. Now I'm moving to the leaves and limbs, setting up a shared bone-stand config for the branch group, bark texture for the tubes, and dark skin tones with a grey ramp for the digits. For limbs I'm sweeping a catmull-spline path with a tapering tube radius for a tapered tube shape.

I'm working out the trunk shape with flared base radii and checking that the fork limbs and top cap overlap cleanly behind the body, since the koala leans against the trunk so any overlap gets hidden from view. I'll double check this from the back angle later.

Now I'm defining twigs as curving catmull-rom paths that dip toward the tip, with leaf frames computed along each twig path so the leaf cards hang naturally from points along the branch.

I'm randomizing each leaf's flow direction horizontally per card, pairing leaves at each node with slight orientation differences, and sizing the leaf cards to mimic eucalyptus proportions with a fine 8x20 pixel texture grid. With roughly 12 twigs carrying 14 leaves apiece plus extra clusters, I'm aiming for around 170 total leaves.

I need to keep twigs clear of the koala's head and ears, so I'm checking that limb tips and outward-growing twigs stay beyond x=0.3 and avoid the region near y=1.45 where the ears sit. I'm also considering a cute detail like a single gum leaf near the koala's mouth, though I'm leaning toward skipping it since it may not be necessary.

I'm planning the plinth decorations instead: gumnuts, fallen leaves, grass, mushrooms, pebbles, a plaque, and a bark curl. For gumnuts I'll merge a small sphere with a flat cylinder cap, making sure geometry attributes match so they can be combined using a buffer geometry merge utility, with colors applied via ramps. I'm also setting texel constants for body and face detail, and sketching the plinth as a lathe shape with a small segment count for a faceted, flat-shaded look.

Now I'm working out the plinth's surface painting -- distinguishing grass from dirt based on surface normal, adding a soil mound near the trunk, and making sure the textured lathe's radius keeps the footprint within bounds so leaves can extend slightly beyond it. I'm about to assemble everything into one large file, being careful with the stick/surface API calls, and sketching a paw-building function I'll implement inline with loops rather than as a separate reusable function.

I need to double check where the Joint type is exported from before importing it.
